title: Divine Holiness
summary: Leviticus 19 grounds Israel’s call to holiness in God’s own holiness. Isaiah 6 gives that language a vivid temple setting: the seraphim proclaim God holy, Isaiah recognizes his uncleanness, and a coal from the altar marks his cleansing before he is sent. First Peter 1 quotes the command to be holy and applies it to the conduct of its readers. Hebrews 12 urges its readers to pursue peace and holiness. The passages connect who God is with the way people are called to live, but they express that connection through different genres and arguments.
historical_context: The references come from different literary settings. Leviticus 19 opens a collection of commands addressed to Israel and grounds its call to holiness in God’s character. Isaiah 6 narrates a prophetic vision of the Lord in the temple, where Isaiah’s confession, cleansing, and commission follow the seraphim’s proclamation. First Peter 1 uses Israel’s holiness command in an exhortation to its readers. Hebrews 12 also exhorts its audience to pursue holiness. The texts show the command being recalled and applied, not one unchanged ritual practice across all these settings.
canonical_context: Leviticus 19 gives Israel the command to be holy because God is holy. Isaiah 6 depicts holiness in a temple vision that leads from confession and cleansing to prophetic service. First Peter 1 quotes the command as guidance for its readers, and Hebrews 12 speaks of holiness as something to pursue. These passages connect divine holiness with human response across the canon while keeping the Torah command, prophetic scene, and later exhortations distinct.
literary_context: The theme appears in a legal exhortation in Leviticus 19, a throne-room vision in Isaiah 6, a letter’s call to conduct in First Peter 1, and a compact exhortation in Hebrews 12. Isaiah’s repeated “holy” intensifies the vision; the scene then moves through the prophet’s confession, cleansing, and commission. First Peter quotes the holiness command, while Hebrews frames holiness alongside peace. The literary form shows whether a passage is commanding, depicting, quoting, or urging holiness.
covenantal_significance: Leviticus 19 connects Israel’s calling with God’s holiness. Isaiah 6 shows that holiness as overwhelming presence, while also depicting cleansing and a commission for the prophet. First Peter 1 carries the command into its readers’ conduct, and Hebrews 12 urges a pursuit of holiness. Together the passages show that divine holiness is not only a description of God; it also shapes the worship, calling, and conduct of those addressed in each text.
canonical_role: Divine Holiness serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Divine Holiness in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
